title: Database Sharding
lesson:
Sharding (also called partitioning) splits a large dataset across multiple database nodes, called shards, each holding a subset of the rows. Where replication (covered earlier) copies the *same* data onto multiple nodes for availability and read throughput, sharding splits the data itself so that no single node has to store or serve the entire dataset. This is what lets a system scale storage and write throughput past what one machine can hold, once vertical scaling (a bigger box) stops being economical or physically possible.

The two common ways to decide which shard a row belongs to are range-based and hash-based partitioning. Range-based partitioning assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (e.g. user IDs 1-1000 on shard A, 1001-2000 on shard B), which keeps range queries and ordered scans efficient but risks hotspots when writes cluster at one end of the range, such as monotonically increasing IDs or timestamps all landing on the newest shard. Hash-based partitioning instead hashes each row's shard key and uses the hash to pick a shard, which spreads load far more evenly but scatters related or sequential keys across shards, making range queries expensive since they now have to fan out to every shard. Consistent hashing, covered previously, is a common technique for the hash-based approach specifically because it limits how many keys have to move when a shard is added or removed, rather than reshuffling nearly everything the way a plain hash-modulo-N scheme would.

Sharding introduces problems that don't exist on a single node. Queries or transactions that need data from more than one shard, such as a join across two tables that live on different shards, either require an expensive scatter-gather across every shard or aren't supported at all. Multi-shard transactions need a distributed transaction protocol (or get avoided by design) since a single node can no longer just wrap the whole operation in a local ACID transaction. Rebalancing, moving data between shards as they grow unevenly or as shards are added, has to be done carefully to avoid downtime or data loss.

Because of these costs, the choice of shard key matters more than almost any other decision in a sharded system. A good shard key spreads both storage and traffic evenly across shards and, ideally, matches the application's query patterns so that most queries only need to touch one shard, for example sharding a multi-tenant SaaS product by tenant/organization ID so each customer's data and queries stay within a single shard. A poor shard key, such as one with skewed access patterns, creates hot shards that take disproportionate load while others sit underused, or forces most queries to become expensive cross-shard fan-outs.

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason a system shards its database?
options: To scale storage and write throughput beyond what a single node can handle
To make ad-hoc queries easier to write
To eliminate the need for backups
To guarantee strong consistency across all nodes
questions.explanation: Sharding splits the dataset itself across nodes so no single machine has to store or serve all of it, which is what lets storage and write throughput scale past one node's limits.

questions.prompt: Hash-based partitioning makes range queries, like "all rows created in March," efficient because keys are spread evenly across shards.
questions.explanation: Hashing deliberately scatters related and sequential keys across shards, so a range query has to fan out to every shard instead of hitting one contiguous chunk.

questions.prompt: The field used to decide which shard a given row is routed to is called the shard ____.
questions.explanation: The shard key is hashed or range-matched to determine which shard a row lives on, so choosing it well is what determines load balance and query locality.

questions.prompt: How does consistent hashing help specifically when a shard is added to or removed from a growing sharded system?
options: It guarantees every shard holds exactly the same number of rows forever
It only remaps the keys near the changed shard instead of reshuffling nearly all keys
It removes the need for a shard key entirely
It makes cross-shard joins as fast as single-node joins
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing places shards and keys on a ring so only the keys adjacent to the changed shard need to move, unlike plain hash-modulo-N which remaps almost everything when the shard count changes.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of adding a new shard under consistent hashing, earliest first.
items: Only the keys that now fall between the new shard and its predecessor on the ring are identified
The new shard is placed onto the hash ring
The new shard begins serving reads and writes for its assigned key range
The identified keys are migrated from their old shard to the new shard
questions.explanation: The new node is placed on the ring first, which determines which contiguous slice of keys now belongs to it, then only that slice is migrated before the new shard starts serving traffic.

questions.prompt: A poorly chosen shard key can cause one shard to receive disproportionate traffic while other shards sit comparatively idle.
questions.explanation: If the shard key doesn't distribute access patterns evenly, for example when one tenant dominates traffic, all of that load lands on a single shard while the rest stay underused.
